cells.tense: The adjustment is happening now, in your hands, as you work.
cells.act: keep the ritual and give it room to change
cells.ask: Take one part of your practice you do the same way each time, keep it, and change one detail of how it's done this month. If the change holds, keep that too, and if the old way was better, put it back.
cells.core:
You've got the mix right, and it shows because it keeps changing. You sense when to add an hour, when to pull back, when to fold in something new, and the practice stays alive rather than stiff. It runs on attention you decide to give it.
The catch is that a practice this fitted to you can seal up if it stops moving. So let one piece of it pass to someone else, or take something they keep and carry it forward in your own way, and count that as the same work. What passes between you is part of the practice. Keep it where you can see it.
cells.sheetLine: The practice holds because it keeps changing.
cells.verb: adjusting the mix as it goes
cells.place: at the bench where you keep the small, repeated practice

cells.tense: You will have smoothed over the next disagreement before it ever gets said.
cells.ask: Pick the next moment you want to smooth over before it's real, and say the thing before it feels ready. Don't wait for the room to settle first.
cells.core:
The tuning has gotten to the moment too early. In your practice you're already deciding what the next version should sound like, and among people you're settling differences before anyone has finished feeling them. It keeps the surface calm and blurs the distinctions that would tell you what's actually there.
What's honest here is blunt: what you feel — annoyance, excitement, the pull toward one thing — is the direction, even when it's inconvenient. Let one real difference stand before you harmonize it, and take one step toward what you actually want rather than what would keep things even. The tuning gets sharper when it has something true to work on.
cells.sheetLine: You're smoothing differences before anyone can feel them.
cells.verb: adjusting the mix as it goes
cells.place: at the bench where you keep the small, repeated practice

cells.tense: You were pulled apart by whatever last engaged you, and you are standing in it still.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Sit with a friend for a while while they're in something hard. Don't fix it, don't bring it back to your own practice, and don't lose your own side while you're there.
cells.core:
Every engagement scatters you, and you don't land anywhere with enough stillness to notice what's happening. No practice gets kept right now, and the last thing that pulled you apart has your attention.
Contact is what brings you back, and it doesn't require you to have anything worked out first. Sit with one person in whatever is hard for them — not fixing it, not making it about your practice, keeping your own side while you're there. Being alongside someone is itself a steadying thing, and it works even when your own center is nowhere in sight. That's the way back in.

cells.tense: You are steadying the room right now without knowing that is what you're doing.
cells.act: learn how the people before you did it
cells.ask: Ask someone who came before you in this practice how they kept it going when it went stale, then try one thing they tell you in your own week.
cells.core:
The adjusting is happening — you sense a room, shift your tone, steady things — and you'd say the work just goes well or the practice runs itself. The hand on the dial is yours, and you haven't been counting it.
Go back to someone who came before you in this and ask how they kept it going. Not for advice on your whole life — just how they handled the part that goes stale. Take one thing they actually did and try it in yours. You come back with something to hold, and it belongs to the practice as much as to the person who handed it over.

cells.verb: adjusting the mix as it goes
cells.place: at the bench where you keep the small, repeated practice

The line that would serve me more than them is any version of 'this is really about reclaiming your authorship' — dropped, since authorship is my word for the mechanism, not theirs. Too Much and Too Little must not mirror each other into a single sentence about balance; one is tuned past the moment, the other standing where nothing is being practiced at all.
